description:
This research project focuses on developing a bilingual (English and Spanish) digital health intervention to support healthy aging among Hispanic/Latino older adults. The goal is to better understand their needs, experiences, and preferences related to stress management, problem-solving, mobility, and overall well-being.

The project uses a community-engaged approach to explore how digital health tools can be more accessible, culturally appropriate, and useful for older adults. Research activities may include literature reviews, developing and reviewing interview guides, organizing qualitative data, and analyzing feedback from participants and healthcare providers.

Under the guidance of the faculty mentor, the graduate team leader will coordinate research activities and mentor two undergraduate researchers. Together, the team will contribute to understanding the needs of older adults and identifying ways to improve the digital health intervention.

Project Overview:

This project investigates the evolution and underlying anatomical mechanisms that allow plants to regenerate from leaf tissue. The study system is the Ledebouriinae, a group of plants within the monocot family Asparagaceae subfamily Scilloideae. Students will generate anatomical slides of plant leaf tissue, analyze the resulting anatomical slides, and analyze data using the R coding language.

description: This project focuses on developing novel optoelectronic materials for neuromorphic synapse devices that emulate the learning and memory functions of biological synapses. The research involves designing and integrating light-responsive semiconductor materials, including organic and perovskite-based materials, into two-terminal device architectures. The optical and electrical properties of the materials will be investigated to achieve wavelength-dependent synaptic responses, plasticity, potentiation/depression, and memory behavior. The developed devices will be further evaluated for their potential in neuromorphic computing and artificial neural network applications, with the goal of enabling low-power, multifunctional, and optically controlled artificial synaptic systems.

description:
Our research team is looking for motivated undergraduate students interested in exploring how chemistry, nanotechnology, and materials science can be used to solve real-world challenges.

Students will work alongside graduate researchers on projects involving the design, synthesis, characterization, and application of advanced materials. Current research areas include developing novel drug-delivery systems, engineering antimicrobial nanomaterials, designing sustainable agricultural technologies, and investigating deep eutectic solvents as alternatives to conventional chemical formulations.

Depending on their interests, students may gain experience with:

- Nanomaterial Synthesis: Developing and optimizing nanoparticles and functional materials.
- Analytical chemistry: Using techniques such as LC-MS, UV-Vis spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, XRD, and electron microscopy.
- Biological applications: Investigating antimicrobial activity and the interactions between materials and biological systems.

Our goal is to provide students with more than laboratory experience. We want to help them develop the scientific independence, technical skills, and critical thinking necessary to become the next generation of researchers and innovators.

description: Many modern drug delivery and agricultural formulations rely on synthetic polymers such as polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) to stabilize and encapsulate active ingredients. While these materials are widely used, there is growing interest in exploring naturally derived alternatives that offer improved sustainability, biodegradability, and compatibility with biological systems. Captin will investigate the use of pectin, a naturally occurring polysaccharide found in plant cell walls, as an alternative encapsulation material. Our goal is to develop and optimize pectin-based formulations capable of protecting active ingredients and controlling their release for potential applications in biomedical technologies and sustainable agriculture.

title: Enhancing Fruit Tree Crops Health Using Probiotic Targeted Delivery System
preferred_quals: Preference will be given to students in the biology department, those who have studied Botany or related courses, or students who are excited about improving plant health

description: Citrus canker is a destructive disease of citrus caused by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri, which produces raised corky lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit that reduce yield and fruit quality. Current management relies largely on copper bactericides, but repeated use can lead to environmental accumulation and copper-tolerant strains. The yeast-like fungus Aureobasidium pullulans, which naturally colonizes plant surfaces, has been successfully used in apple orchards to control fire blight caused by Erwinia amylovora through competitive exclusion on blossoms. Applying A. pullulans to citrus foliage may similarly suppress X. citri colonization, offering a promising biological control strategy to complement existing citrus canker management practices.

description:
Wildfires pose an increasing threat to ecosystems, wildlife, and communities, creating a need for innovative materials that can reduce the flammability of vegetation and limit fire spread.

PhyroProtect is a materials science research project focused on investigating a novel formulation designed to reduce the flammability of plant materials. Our team will evaluate the material's ability to delay ignition, reduce flame propagation, and improve the fire resistance of treated vegetation.

Students involved in this project will gain hands-on experience in materials science, experimental design, formulation development, and laboratory testing. Research will include evaluating material properties, studying interactions with plant surfaces, and comparing the flammability of treated and untreated plant samples under controlled conditions.

description: This project examines why individuals with similar training, experience, procedures, and access to information can make different decisions in high-stakes security environments. Existing research has identified cognitive biases, stress, workload, expertise, and organizational factors as important influences on decision-making, but these factors do not fully explain variation between similarly situated individuals. The project will investigate the cognitive and human factors that may account for these differences, with particular attention to how individuals interpret information, verify automated or uncertain information, adapt under pressure, and recover from potential judgment errors. The research is expected to use a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative analysis with qualitative interviews or decision-based case analysis. The broader goal is to develop a clearer explanation of individual differences in security decision-making that can contribute to research on human factors, cognitive security, and organizational resilience.

title: Development of a Smart Low-Profile Variable-Stiffness Ankle-Foot Prosthesis
affiliation: College of Engineering and Computer Science
preferred_quals: Junior and Senior Mechanical Engineering students
SOLIDWORKS 3D CAD designing
Coding
Finite Element Analysis
quals_raw:
Preferred: Junior and Senior Mechanical Engineering students
SOLIDWORKS 3D CAD designing, Coding, Finite Element Analysis
description:
More than 60 million people worldwide live with lower-limb amputations. The loss of a functional ankle joint often leads to complications such as impaired mobility, back pain, and postural changes. Robotic ankle-foot prostheses (AFPs) have been developed to replicate the biomechanical properties of the biological ankle and Achilles tendon, providing support for dynamic tasks such as stiffness adjustment and energy storage and return.
However, most robotic AFPs require increased height to accommodate actuators and mechanical components. This added height affects the prosthesis’ overall size, weight, and appearance, which can disrupt the user’s natural gait and hinder the device’s integration with their body. One of the major challenges in AFP design is creating a low-profile mechanism that preserves the maximum residual limb length. Research studies have shown that individuals with longer residual limbs achieve more stable gait patterns, especially when navigating uneven terrain or performing dynamic activities. This improved stability enhances user confidence and promotes greater independence and mobility.
The goal of this project is to finalize the engineering of a low-profile, variable-stiffness AFP in the Rehabilitation Engineering and Assistive Device Lab (REAL) under the supervision of Dr. Choi. We aim to develop a compact and lightweight AFP using an adjustable cantilever beam design. The first phase of the project will focus on three primary aims:
• Aim 1: Design and develop a compact, and lightweight AFP with adjustable stiffness.
• Aim 2: Adapt the elastic cantilever beam design for scalable and feasible manufacturing, validated through finite element analysis (FEA).
• Aim 3: Implement novel control mechanisms to create a smart, low-profile AFP.
In this phase, the team will also produce initial commercial-style prototypes for preliminary evaluation. Phase 2 will expand to developing an AFP care framework and testing smart techniques through human subject evaluations.

description: This project focuses on the development of a low-cost wearable smart insole intended for at-home gait monitoring. The system integrates plantar-pressure sensors with an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to collect synchronized foot-loading and motion data during walking. A preliminary breadboard prototype has been developed using an Adafruit nRF52840 Feather, six pressure-sensing channels, an LSM6DS3TR-C IMU, and onboard microSD data storage. Following integration, the device will undergo walking evaluations to assess data quality, repeatability, battery life, and user comfort.

affiliation: College of Community Innovation and Education

description:
Creating Web Apps That Limit Attention Harm Based on the A.S.M. Models is an applied research and development project in which students will design, build, and deploy a functional web application using Base44. Each project must address a clearly defined form of attention harm—such as compulsive use patterns, manipulative engagement design, excessive notifications, distraction, or other digital experiences that undermine users’ well-being, agency, or focus.

Students will use the A.S.M. models as the guiding framework for their application’s purpose, user experience, features, and safeguards. The final product must demonstrate how intentional web design can reduce harmful attention practices while promoting more responsible, transparent, and user-centered digital interaction.

After deployment, each student’s application will be tested through C.A.S. to evaluate whether it meets the applicable A.S.M. standards. This assessment will examine whether the app’s design, functionality, and user-flow decisions align with the project’s stated attention-harm reduction goals. Students should be prepared to document their design rationale, identify the specific standards their app addresses, and respond to findings generated through the C.A.S. testing process.

Students are also required to present their completed project during Research Week in the Spring. Presentations should explain the attention-related issue the app addresses, the A.S.M. standards used to guide development, the Base44 deployment process, the C.A.S. testing results, and any changes made to strengthen compliance with the standards.

Required deliverables
A deployed web application built in Base44

A written explanation of the attention harm the app is designed to limit

Documentation showing how the app applies the A.S.M. models

C.A.S. testing and a review of the app’s results against A.S.M. standards

A Spring Research Week presentation demonstrating the app, findings, and design rationale

*This is not for someone who lacks time management skills*

description:
BACKGROUND: When landing on a lunar surface, damage occurs due to the impact of the nozzle plume on the granular surface material. The reduced gravity (0.166 g or 1.625 m/s2) environment of the moon and the absence of significant atmospheric pressure (10-10 Torr or below) complicate these physics. Understanding the physics of the rarefied and transition flow, and the influence on the surface material, is vital for enabling technology which will allow for repeated co-located landings.

RESEARCH PROBLEM: Landers can have under-, over-, or perfectly-expanded nozzle designs which correspond to over-, under-, or perfectly-expanded plumes, respectively. The shape of the plume is also influenced by the atmospheric pressure of the landing site – in higher ambient pressure regimes, plumes can become collimated, ‘concentrating’ down, for example, a plume that would have been over-expanded into a perfectly-expanded plume. We propose that the process of collimation likely changes the structure of the plume itself, and that we should work to isolate the plume shape and atmospheric pressure variables.

APPROACH: Our lab has an existing experimental setup – the Gas-Regolith Interaction Testbed (GRIT) – which is a drop-tower (microgravity) vacuum chamber experiment. GRIT has a solenoid-controlled opening which allows atmosphere to enter the chamber (creating our nozzle plume), and we place regolith simulants to replicate the granular lunar surface material. We will design* and install a set of nozzles so that we can study over-, perfectly-, and under-expanded plumes in a range of atmospheric conditions. Since our nozzle does not have to support a lander, we can purposely design inefficient nozzles that would not be used in real missions to experimentally explore the parameter space.

* Please note that the design phase is complete, and we are now focused on data collection and analysis.

STUDENT BENEFIT: One of the best ways to explore what makes for an efficient nozzle design is to purposely design many inefficient nozzles. This project could be the basis for a great engineering senior design project and will give students experience with designing and constructing nozzles, then collecting and analyzing experimental data regarding the nozzle performance in different environments.

description: Conversational artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used in contexts that rely on emotional and social engagement, including education, mental health support, and companionship. Users frequently describe these systems as empathetic or understanding, suggesting that language-based interaction alone can elicit social responses typically reserved for human partners. However, the mechanisms underlying this perceived emotional connection remain poorly understood. Current approaches of-ten attribute these effects to anthropomorphic interpretations or emergent “AI empathy” without isolating the specific features that drive such perceptions. This gap limits our ability to evaluate how humans cognitively interpret artificial agents and obscures the boundary between perceived understanding and genuine social cognition. Building on this link, this study examines how language-driven mirroring engages neural and autonomic systems typically involved in social cognition and affective processing, and how individual differences modulate susceptibility to HIAG-related dynamics. Specifically, this project asks whether syntactic linguistic mirroring in conversational AI is sufficient to elicit measurable neural and autonomic responses associated with social engage-ment, and whether individual differences shape susceptibility to this effect. By isolating linguistic structure from semantic content and linking it to neurophysiological responses, this work aims to clarify how social cognition can be evoked by artificial systems, with implications for neuroscience, human–AI interaction, and ethical AI design.

description:
This study evaluates the cognitive and emotional mechanisms involved in processing accented English speech and whether accent comprehension engages processes similar to bilingual language switching. Specifically, the study compares two listener groups:

English Monolinguals: Individuals with minimal foreign language exposure.

Bilinguals: Individuals proficient in English and at least one additional language.

The study also evaluates responses across four accent conditions presented within subjects:

American Accent: Baseline / highly familiar condition.
British Accent: Moderately familiar accent condition.
Indian Accent: Less familiar accent condition.
Russian Accent: Least familiar accent condition.

Stimuli being evaluated:
AI-generated English sentences presented in four accent blocks (American, British, Indian, Russian) during a laboratory listening task. Accent blocks are counterbalanced across participants. Sentences include both simple and complex grammatical structures. Accent switch and repetition trials are embedded to assess processing dynamics.

Instruments being administered (not evaluated for psychometric properties):
• Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q)
• Big Five Personality Inventory
• Need for Cognitive Closure – Short Form
• Tolerance of Ambiguity – Short Form
• Subjective Listening Rating Scales (difficulty, effort, comfort, conflict, expectation match, accent familiarity)
• Speaker Evaluation Ratings (intelligence, competence, friendliness, clarity, trustworthiness, likeability, confidence)

Neurophysiological measures:
• EEG (event-related potentials associated with phonological processing and expectation violations)
• ECG-derived heart rate variability (autonomic regulation and cognitive load)
• Galvanic Skin Response (sympathetic arousal)

Physiological signals are used to assess cognitive load and emotional arousal during accent processing. The study evaluates listener responses to accent type and language background, not the diagnostic validity of the physiological recording systems

description:
Stress responses vary considerably across individuals, yet the neurological mechanisms underlying these differences remain incompletely understood. Research suggests that hemispheric lateralization, the differential activation of left versus right brain hemispheres, plays a critical role in stress processing. Studies have linked left-hemispheric activation to positive affective states and right-hemispheric activation to negative emotions and withdrawal behaviors (Davidson et al., 1990; Hamid et al., 2015). However, conflicting findings indicate the right hemisphere may also process certain positive emotions related to arousal (Cao et al., 2020), highlighting the need for research examining hemispheric activity under ecologically valid stressful conditions.

This study investigates hemispheric lateralization patterns during acute stress induced by high cognitive load using a driving simulation. Participants will complete a challenging driving simulation while wearing a wireless EEG to monitor hemispheric activity across frontal, temporal, and parietal regions. Baseline recordings and subjective stress ratings will be collected for comparison.

This research addresses a significant gap by examining hemispheric activity during naturalistic cognitive stress rather than passive viewing of emotional stimuli, potentially informing targeted stress-reduction interventions.

description:
This is a well-designed study proposal examining how neurodivergent individuals (those with ADHD, dyslexia, or strong visual-spatial abilities) organize digital files compared to neurotypical users. The research investigates whether different cognitive profiles align with different organizational paradigms, spatial/piling, hierarchical/filing, flat/search-based, or hybrid approaches.
The study hypothesizes that individuals with ADHD may prefer spatial organization due to working memory considerations, while those with dyslexia or visual-spatial strengths may favor visual approaches over text-heavy hierarchical systems. A key question is whether current file management systems systematically disadvantage neurodivergent users by forcing paradigms misaligned with their cognitive strengths.
Using 240 participants across four groups, the methodology employs visual stimuli of organizational paradigms, NASA-TLX cognitive load ratings, and preference assessments. The theoretical contribution extends cognitive fit theory to file management, reframing the question from "how can neurodivergent users adapt" to "how might systems accommodate cognitive diversity.

description:
Deep Multimodal Terrain Recognition for Safe Robotic and Wearable Mobility refers to a perception framework that integrates multiple complementary sensors—such as cameras, IMUs, LiDAR, and proprioceptive signals—to accurately classify and predict terrain conditions during locomotion. By leveraging deep learning–based multimodal fusion, the system captures both visual appearance and motion/force cues, enabling robust recognition of stairs, slopes, uneven ground, grass, gravel, and other challenging environments.

This multimodal approach improves reliability compared to single‑sensor systems, especially in real‑world conditions where lighting, occlusion, or sensor noise can degrade performance. Research in multimodal fusion for robot navigation shows that combining RGB images with LiDAR or IMU data significantly enhances perception robustness and navigation accuracy in complex environments .

For robotic platforms, the system supports safer autonomous navigation by providing terrain‑aware decision‑making and traversability estimation. For wearable mobility devices—such as powered prosthetic legs, exoskeletons, and orthoses—it enables predictive control strategies that adjust joint impedance, torque, or gait mode before the user encounters a new terrain, reducing fall risk and improving mobility confidence.

description: This project investigates how Lactobacillus species and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) mitigate DNA damage and chronic inflammation associated with Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) and Barrett’s esophagus. Who Should Apply?

Minimum Requirements
GPA of 3.0 or higher
Sophomore standing or above

Preferred Background
Completion of Organic Chemistry
Interest in chemistry, atmospheric science, environmental science, climate science, or related STEM disciplines

No previous research experience is required. We welcome students who are eager to learn, dependable, and enthusiastic about hands-on laboratory work and data analysis. Comprehensive training in research methods and instrumentation will be provided.
description:
Wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe across the globe, producing vast amounts of smoke that can travel thousands of miles and impact both local and global air quality. Smoke particles, known as aerosols, play a critical role in Earth's atmosphere. They can scatter and absorb sunlight, influencing climate and visibility, and they can also act as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), tiny particles that help water vapor condense into cloud droplets. Because clouds strongly affect weather patterns, precipitation, and climate, understanding how wildfire smoke behaves in the atmosphere is an important scientific challenge.
This research project focuses on a group of organic compounds known as phenolic acids (including vanillic acid, syringic acid, and ferulic acid), which are commonly produced during biomass burning and are frequently used as tracers of wildfire emissions. While these compounds are widely detected in wildfire smoke, scientists still know surprisingly little about how they change after being released into the atmosphere and how those changes affect their ability to seed clouds.
In this project, we recreate key atmospheric processes in the laboratory and investigate how wildfire-derived particles evolve over time. Aerosol particles are generated from phenolic acid solutions, size-selected using advanced instrumentation, and exposed to oxidizing conditions that mimic atmospheric aging. We then measure how efficiently these particles form cloud droplets before and after aging using state-of-the-art aerosol and cloud condensation nuclei instrumentation. Changes in chemical composition are characterized using Direct Analysis in Real Time Mass Spectrometry (DART-MS).
Our preliminary findings reveal a fascinating phenomenon: freshly generated particles have a very low ability to attract water and form cloud droplets, but atmospheric oxidation significantly enhances their cloud-forming potential. These results suggest that chemical processing in the atmosphere can dramatically alter the environmental and climate impacts of wildfire smoke.
This project offers students the opportunity to contribute to research at the intersection of atmospheric chemistry, environmental science, climate science, and analytical chemistry, while helping answer important questions about the effects of wildfires on our changing planet.

Future Research Opportunities

Students participating in this project may help explore several exciting research directions, including:
Investigating the effects of hydroxyl (OH) radical oxidation, one of the most important chemical aging processes in the atmosphere.
Studying how particle mixtures and surface coatings influence cloud formation.
Expanding the research to additional organic compounds commonly found in wildfire smoke.
Exploring the connections between aerosol chemistry, air quality, and climate impacts.

What Students Involved in this Research Project Will Learn

This project provides extensive hands-on research experience and training in modern atmospheric chemistry techniques. Students will have opportunities to:
Generate and characterize aerosol particles.
Operate advanced scientific instrumentation used in environmental and atmospheric research.
Measure cloud condensation nuclei activity and particle hygroscopicity.
Analyze experimental data and interpret scientific results.
Learn principles of atmospheric chemistry, aerosol science, and climate-related research.
Develop skills in scientific communication, problem-solving, and laboratory safety.
Work closely with graduate students and faculty mentors in a collaborative research environment.
Students who demonstrate strong interest and commitment may have opportunities to present their work at undergraduate research conferences and contribute to publications.

description: This project aims to determine which component(s) of the 8-week Physiofeedback Exercise Program (PEER) is most effective in improving physical activity levels in community-dwelling older adults. The PEER is comprised of three components: physiofeedback, cognitive reframing, and group exercise, and each group will receive a random combination of these three components. This longitudinal study will involve multiple visits (baseline, post-intervention, 6-month follow-up, 12-month follow-up) over a 15-month time period.

title: Exploring AI-Supported Accessibility for Students with Chronic Physical Disabilities in Higher Education
affiliation: College of Community Innovation and Education
description:
The purpose of this study is to examine how students with chronic physical disabilities experience the tension between fluctuating access needs and the predictable structures of higher education. Chronic disabilities are often episodic and unpredictable, with symptoms and access needs that may vary daily, weekly, or across academic contexts. However, higher education systems are frequently organized around predictability, including fixed attendance policies, standardized deadlines, scheduled participation expectations, timed assessments, and accommodation processes that often require advance documentation and planning. This study will investigate how students with chronic disabilities navigate these structures and how AI-supported tools may support, complicate, or reshape accessibility practices.

This study will use a qualitative-dominant mixed methods design with participatory design elements. The study will begin with an online questionnaire to gather descriptive information about participants’ chronic physical disability experiences, academic access needs, experiences with higher education accessibility structures, and familiarity with AI-supported tools. Participants will then be invited to complete a semi-structured interview focused on their experiences with fluctuating access needs, barriers to flexibility, accommodation processes, disclosure concerns, and perceptions of AI-supported accessibility. During the interview, participants will also be given brief scenarios or design prompts related to possible AI-supported accessibility tools, such as flexible planning tools, low-burden communication supports, workload management tools, or systems for navigating course expectations.

The research questions guiding this study are:

1. How do students with chronic physical disabilities describe the relationship between fluctuating access needs and predictable structures within higher education?
2. What barriers and supports do students with chronic physical disabilities identify in relation to flexibility, accommodation processes, participation expectations, and academic workload?
3. How do students with chronic physical disabilities perceive the potential benefits, limitations, and risks of AI-supported accessibility tools in higher education?

Required: CITI Human Subjects Research Group 2 Social/Behavioral Research
description:
The purpose of this study is to characterize within-person variations in physical activity and exercise behaviors across the menstrual cycle phases. This project aims to examine whether muscular strength performance differs across the early follicular, ovulatory, and mid-luteal phases of the menstrual cycle, and to determine the extent to which physiological factors (heart rate variability and sleep quality) versus psychological factors (mood, self-efficacy, and perceived exertion) explain variation in strength performance and exercise outcomes across the menstrual cycle phases.
The study requires participation over one full menstrual cycle (approximately 30–35 days), including wearing a Garmin watch, completing surveys twice a day, and coming in for two in-person visits. An optional strength training sub-study requires three additional in-person visits to complete a 5-repetition maximum (5RM) of the following lifts: Barbell Back Squat, Barbell Bench Press, and Barbell Deadlift.

description:
This study investigates the intention-behavior gap in postpartum women's physical activity, utilizing the Theory of Planned Behavior as a framework. Our goal is to understand how postpartum women think about returning to exercising, what motivates them, and what obstacles prevent them from doing so.

The study uses semi-structured interviews and a 14-day activity monitoring phase to capture attitudes and real-world behaviors. Participants will do a Zoom interview followed by two weeks of activity tracking with an Apple Watch and the Pathverse app. The study will begin with recruiting postpartum mothers in Orlando, with the possibility to increase participation throughout the United States. This study's findings will contribute to maternal health research and inform future programs aimed at increasing postpartum physical activity in postpartum women.
